1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. TTL: time to live; EMR: Elastic MapReduce; IAM: Identity and Access Management; ORC: Optimized Row Columnar; KMS: Key Management Service; IA: Infrequent Access; MFA: multi-factor authentication; WORM: write once, read many; RDS: Relational Database Service; AZ: Availability Zone; RPO: recovery point objective; EBS: Elastic Block Store; EFS: Elastic File System; EC2: Elastic Compute Cloud; SNS: Simple Notification Service

  • Move data between Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift with COPY and UNLOAD
  • Use S3 Lifecycle policies to change storage tiers and expire data
  • Manage S3 versioning and DynamoDB TTL
  • Delete data to meet business and legal requirements
  • Protect data with the right resiliency and availability

2Loading and Unloading Between S3 and Redshift (skill 2.3.1)

Running case

Kestrel Freight Ages Its Data

  • Last month's orders are queried daily; older months almost never
  • Raw files may be deleted after two years, but invoices must be kept seven years
  • A customer asks Kestrel to erase their personal data
  • Your job: keep hot data fast, cold data cheap, and deletions provable

Command Direction Remember
COPY S3 → Redshift (also from DynamoDB, EMR and remote hosts) Parallel load across slices; IAM role to read S3; formats CSV, JSON, Avro, Parquet, ORC; compression options (GZIP, ZSTD, BZIP2, LZOP); manifest file lists exact files; MAXERROR; splittable and similar-size files load fastest (Module 1)
UNLOAD Redshift → S3 Writes result files in parallel (several files); can write Parquet, partition by columns, encrypt with KMS, overwrite, and write a manifest; use it to archive old data or hand data to the lake
Auto-copy / COPY JOB [Beyond the guide] S3 → Redshift, automatically Loads new files from an S3 prefix as they arrive
  • Typical lifecycle: hot data in Redshift tables → UNLOAD older partitions to S3 as Parquet → delete them from Redshift → still queryable through Redshift Spectrum (Module 6)
  • Loading best practices: COPY, not row inserts; one COPY per table over a prefix; compress; verify loaded row counts and errors (STL_LOAD_ERRORS)
Exam tip

"Move old rows out of Redshift to cheap storage and still query them" → UNLOAD to S3 as Parquet, then query with Redshift Spectrum. "Load many files fast" → COPY (not INSERT).

3S3 Lifecycle Policies: Tiering and Expiring (skills 2.3.2 and 2.3.3)

Lifecycle actions

Action What it does
Transition Moves objects to a cheaper storage class after N days
Expiration Deletes current objects after N days (in a versioned bucket it adds a delete marker)
Noncurrent version transition / expiration Moves or permanently deletes older versions after N days
Abort incomplete multipart uploads Cleans up unfinished uploads
Filters By prefix, tags, object size (ObjectSizeGreaterThan / LessThan)

Rules to remember [Verify live]

  • Waterfall model: objects move down the classes: Standard → Standard-IA → Glacier Instant Retrieval → Glacier Flexible Retrieval → Glacier Deep Archive (also One Zone-IA and Intelligent-Tiering); Deep Archive is one way (restore, then copy, to move back)
  • Objects smaller than 128 KB do not transition by default (the request cost can exceed the saving); change it with an object size filter
  • Minimum storage durations are charged on early exit: Standard-IA 30 days, Glacier Instant and Flexible 90, Deep Archive 180; you cannot move an object on before its minimum period has passed in one rule
  • Glacier overhead: each archived object adds about 40 KB of metadata (8 KB at Standard rates, 32 KB at the archive rate): combine many small objects before archiving
  • Archived objects are not instantly available: restore first (Flexible Retrieval: expedited 1–5 minutes, standard 3–5 hours, bulk 5–12 hours; Deep Archive: standard 12 hours, bulk 48 hours)
  • Lifecycle runs asynchronously (a delay between the rule date and the physical change; billing follows the rule date for archive classes)
  • Intelligent-Tiering moves objects automatically when the access pattern is unknown (objects under 128 KB are not tiered)
Exam tip

"Keep data 90 days for fast access, then archive for years at the lowest cost, then delete" → an S3 Lifecycle rule: transition to Glacier classes, then expire. "Unknown or changing access pattern" → S3 Intelligent-Tiering.

4Versioning and DynamoDB TTL (skill 2.3.4)

S3 versioning

  • Versioning keeps every version of an object; an overwrite creates a new version, a delete adds a delete marker (the older versions remain and cost storage)
  • Protects against accidental delete and overwrite; you can restore an earlier version
  • States: unversioned, enabled, suspended (a bucket cannot go back to unversioned)
  • To really delete, delete specific versions or use lifecycle rules for noncurrent versions (expire after N days, keep the last N versions)
  • Add MFA delete and S3 Object Lock (WORM, retention and legal hold) for tamper-proof retention [Beyond the guide]
  • Versioning plus replication supports recovery and disaster protection

DynamoDB TTL (time to live)

  • TTL deletes expired items automatically: enable it on a table and name a TTL attribute holding an expiry time as a Number in Unix epoch seconds
  • Expired items are removed in the background, typically within a few days after expiry, without using write capacity; until then they can still be read, so filter them out of queries
  • Deletions appear in DynamoDB Streams as service deletions, so a stream consumer can archive expired items to S3; with global tables the delete is replicated
  • Use TTL for sessions, temporary records and old telemetry
Exam tip

"Automatically remove DynamoDB items after 30 days at no throughput cost" → TTL with an epoch-seconds attribute. "Recover an accidentally overwritten S3 object" → versioning.

5Deleting Data to Meet Business and Legal Needs (skill 2.3.5)

  • Why delete: retention schedules, privacy laws (for example a right to erasure), contracts, and cost; keep data only as long as it is needed, and keep it as long as the law requires
  • Retention versus deletion: legal hold and WORM (S3 Object Lock) stop deletion; a retention policy says when deletion must happen
  • Automate: S3 Lifecycle expiration, DynamoDB TTL, scheduled deletes in Redshift and RDS, backup retention settings
  • Deleting from files in a lake is hard: immutable files (Parquet) must be rewritten; Apache Iceberg row-level deletes (and S3 Tables) make targeted erasure practical
  • Copies matter: erase from every copy: replicas, backups and snapshots, derived tables, caches, logs; a delete marker or a soft delete is not erasure
  • Prove it: log the deletion (CloudTrail, job logs) and keep an audit record without the personal data
  • Encryption helps [Beyond the guide]: deleting a KMS key makes data encrypted under it unreadable (crypto-shredding), but key deletion has a waiting period and affects everything under that key
Exam tip

"Remove one customer's data from a Parquet lake on request" → Iceberg row-level delete (or rewrite the affected files), and remove it from backups and copies, not a lifecycle rule.

6Resiliency and Availability of Stored Data (skill 2.3.6)

Store Protection Remember
Amazon S3 Designed for 11 nines durability, data across multiple AZs; versioning; replication (same-Region or cross-Region); Object Lock Replication needs versioning; S3 Glacier classes keep the same durability
Amazon DynamoDB Multi-AZ by default; point-in-time recovery (PITR) up to 35 days; on-demand backups; global tables (multi-Region, active-active) PITR restores to a new table
Amazon RDS / Aurora Multi-AZ (standby for failover); automated backups (0 to 35 days) with point-in-time restore; manual snapshots; read replicas; Aurora storage is replicated six ways across three AZs Restores create a new instance
Amazon Redshift Automated and manual snapshots, cross-Region snapshot copy, Multi-AZ for RA3 clusters, backups to S3 Choose retention to match the RPO
Amazon EBS / EFS EBS snapshots; EFS is multi-AZ with backups and lifecycle to IA
AWS Backup Central backup service: backup plans (schedule and retention), vaults, cross-Region and cross-account copies, Vault Lock (WORM) across S3, DynamoDB, RDS, Aurora, EFS, EBS, Redshift and more One policy for many services
  • RPO (recovery point objective): how much data you can lose (time between backups); RTO (recovery time objective): how long recovery may take
  • Choose the strategy by RPO and RTO: backups (cheapest, slowest), cross-Region replication and global tables (lowest RPO and RTO)
  • Test restores: an untested backup is not a recovery plan
  • Availability versus durability: availability = can you reach it now (Multi-AZ, replicas); durability = will the data survive (replication, backups)
Exam tip

"Centrally manage backup schedules and retention across S3, RDS, DynamoDB and EFS, with cross-Region copies" → AWS Backup. "Restore a DynamoDB table to any second in the last 35 days" → point-in-time recovery.

7Exam Q&A

7.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Kestrel Freight keeps the last 12 months of order data in Amazon Redshift. Older data is rarely queried but must remain queryable. What is the most cost-effective approach?

  • AKeep all the data in Redshift and keep adding nodes as the data grows
  • BExport older data to CSV files on Amazon EBS volumes of an EC2 instance
  • CDelete older data permanently once it is a year old
  • DUNLOAD older partitions to S3 as Parquet, delete them from Redshift, and query them with Spectrum
Show the answer

Answer: D. UNLOAD writes older data to cheap S3 in a columnar format, and Spectrum lets Redshift users still query it without loading it.

S2Objects in an S3 bucket must stay in Standard for 30 days, move to an archive class for 7 years, and then be deleted automatically. What should be configured?

  • AA Lambda function that a person runs by hand each month to move the old files
  • BS3 Transfer Acceleration enabled on the bucket
  • CAn S3 Lifecycle rule with transition and expiration actions
  • DS3 event notifications sent to an SNS topic
Show the answer

Answer: C. Lifecycle rules transition objects between storage classes and expire them by age without code.

S3A DynamoDB table holds user sessions that should disappear after 24 hours at no extra throughput cost. What should be used?

  • AA nightly job that scans the table and calls DeleteItem
  • BTTL with an attribute that holds the expiry time in Unix epoch seconds
  • CA global secondary index on the session start time
  • DDynamoDB Accelerator with a shorter item cache time
Show the answer

Answer: B. TTL deletes expired items in the background without consuming write capacity; the attribute must be a Number in epoch seconds.

S4A customer requests erasure of their personal data. The data is in Parquet files in S3, in Redshift and in backups. Which TWO actions are part of a correct approach? (Select TWO.)

  • AChange the bucket's storage class to Glacier
  • BDisable logging so the request cannot be traced
  • CUse Apache Iceberg row-level deletes (or rewrite the affected files) for the lake data
  • DRely on a delete marker in a versioned bucket
  • EDelete the data from every store and copy, including backups and derived datasets, according to policy
Show the answer

Answer: C, E. Erasure must reach all copies, and immutable files need row-level deletes or rewrites. A delete marker only hides the object, archiving keeps the data, and disabling logging removes the proof.

S5A company wants one policy to back up S3, RDS, DynamoDB and EFS, with copies in another Region and WORM protection. Which service fits?

  • AAWS DataSync
  • BAmazon Macie
  • CAWS Backup
  • DAWS Config
Show the answer

Answer: C. AWS Backup centralizes backup plans across services and supports cross-Region copy and Vault Lock.

8Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
COPY / UNLOAD COPY S3 → Redshift in parallel (manifest, compression, formats); UNLOAD Redshift → S3 (Parquet, partitions, KMS); UNLOAD + Spectrum for cold data
S3 Lifecycle Transition (waterfall, one-way to Deep Archive), expiration, noncurrent versions, abort multipart; < 128 KB not transitioned by default; minimum durations 30 / 90 / 180 days
Retrieval Flexible: 1–5 min / 3–5 h / 5–12 h; Deep Archive: 12 h / 48 h
Versioning Every version kept; delete = delete marker; cannot revert to unversioned; lifecycle for noncurrent versions; Object Lock for WORM
TTL Epoch-seconds Number; deleted within a few days, no write capacity; shows in Streams
Deleting Retention schedules; all copies and backups; Iceberg row-level delete; delete marker ≠ erasure; log the proof
Resilience S3 11 nines, versioning, replication; DynamoDB PITR 35 days, global tables; RDS Multi-AZ, backups 0–35 days; Redshift snapshots and cross-Region copy; AWS Backup central
